key_terms.meaning: Updates parameters θ ← θ − η∇θJ(θ), where η is learning rate and ∇J is the loss gradient.
Step size η in parameter updates; too high leads to divergence, too low makes training very slow.
Point where gradient is zero but loss is higher than the global minimum; gradient descent can stall there.
Estimates the full gradient from one random sample per step; fast and noisy per update.
Estimates the full gradient from a small subset of m samples; balances update noise and compute cost.
Keeps velocity v ← βv − η∇J(θ), then θ ← θ + v; β is usually 0.9, smoothing updates.
Evaluates gradient at lookahead point θ + βv first: v ← βv − η∇J(θ+βv), then θ ← θ + v.
Accumulates squared gradients and scales each learning rate as η/√(G+ε); good for sparse data but decays too much.
Uses moving average E[g²] = ρE[g²] + (1−ρ)g² to adapt each weight's learning rate; avoids AdaGrad's aggressive decay.
Combines momentum m and squared gradient v with bias correction; update Δθ = −η m̂/(√v̂+ε).
Gradients shrink exponentially across layers, so early layers learn very slowly.
Gradients grow exponentially, causing huge parameter updates, divergence, or NaN loss.
Samples weights with variance 2/(n_in + n_out) for symmetric activations such as tanh or sigmoid.
Samples weights with variance 2/n_in for ReLU networks to preserve activation variance.
Normalizes each mini-batch activation to zero mean and unit variance, then learns scale γ and shift β.
Randomly zeros units with probability p during training and scales kept units by 1/(1−p) at test.
Adds λ Σ w² to the loss, penalizing large weights and limiting model capacity.
Halts training when validation loss stops improving and restores the best stored weights.
Creates label-preserving variations such as flips, crops, and rotations to enlarge the effective training set.
Systematic search over learning rate, batch size, layers, and regularization using validation performance.

takeaways: Gradient descent is the base optimizer, but one global learning rate and poor loss surfaces can make it slow or stuck.
Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent usually gives the best practical speed-generalization trade-off.
Momentum and Nesterov momentum build velocity from past gradients to damp oscillations and speed descent.
Adaptive optimizers give each weight its own learning rate from gradient history; Adam is a common default.
Vanishing and exploding gradients arise from repeated multiplication through deep layers; ReLU, initialization, and batch normalization reduce them.
Regularization methods such as L2, dropout, and early stopping attack overfitting through different mechanisms.
Data augmentation and hyperparameter tuning are essential parts of training, not optional extras.
Bias-variance tradeoff explains overfitting; validation and regularization help choose the right capacity.
bank_note: Long-answer questions commonly require stating update equations, comparing optimizers on noisy or sparse gradients, and connecting initialization, normalization, and regularization choices to vanishing gradients and generalization.

bank.q: Define the gradient descent update rule and explain its main limitations. Compare full-batch, stochastic, and mini-batch gradient descent in terms of update noise, speed, memory, and generalization.
outline: State θ ← θ − η∇J(θ) with learning rate η and loss J.
Limitations: fixed learning rate sensitivity, local minima, plateaus, no per-weight scaling.
Full-batch uses exact gradient but is slow and memory-heavy.
Stochastic uses one sample, high variance but fast per step.
Mini-batch uses m samples, balances variance and compute; smaller batches often generalize better.
Mention batch size trade-off and practical range.

bank.q: Write the standard momentum update and the Nesterov accelerated gradient update. Explain why momentum accelerates training and how Nesterov improves gradient evaluation.
outline: Standard: v ← βv − η∇J(θ); θ ← θ + v.
Velocity accumulates past gradients; β near 0.9 damps oscillation.
Nesterov: v ← βv − η∇J(θ + βv); θ ← θ + v.
Nesterov looks ahead before measuring gradient, so the update is more responsive.
Compare behaviour on a narrow valley or noisy gradient sequence.

bank.q: Write the update equations for AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam. Compare their per-parameter learning rate behaviour and state one practical scenario for each.
outline: AdaGrad: accumulate G ← G + g², update Δθ = −η g/√(G+ε).
RMSProp: maintain E[g²] = ρE[g²] + (1−ρ)g², update Δθ = −η g/√(E[g²]+ε).
Adam: maintain m and v, bias-correct m̂ and v̂, update Δθ = −η m̂/(√v̂+ε).
AdaGrad suits sparse features but decays too much; RMSProp suits nonstationary problems; Adam is robust and widely used.

bank.q: Explain the causes of vanishing and exploding gradients in deep feedforward networks. Describe three mitigation strategies: ReLU activation, careful weight initialization, and batch normalization.
outline: Repeated Jacobian multiplication through layers; eigenvalues >1 explode, eigenvalues <1 vanish.
Sigmoid/tanh saturation causes small derivatives; small initial weights contribute to vanishing.
ReLU has derivative 1 in the positive region, reducing vanishing.
Xavier and He initialization maintain variance forward and backward.
Batch normalization keeps pre-activations bounded and reduces internal covariate shift.
Optional: gradient clipping for exploding gradients.

bank.q: Write the batch normalization operation for a mini-batch and describe its training versus inference behaviour. Explain the role of learned scale γ and shift β.
outline: Compute mini-batch mean μ and variance σ².
Normalize x̂ = (x − μ)/√(σ² + ε).
Apply y = γ x̂ + β with learnable parameters γ and β.
Training uses batch statistics; inference uses running or fixed average statistics.
γ and β allow the network to undo normalization if needed.

bank.q: Compare L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping as methods to reduce overfitting in neural networks.
outline: Define overfitting as low training loss but high validation/test loss.
L2 adds λ Σ w² to loss; gradient gets 2λw term, shrinking weights.
Dropout randomly zeros units with probability p during training, with inverted scaling at test.
Early stopping monitors validation loss, uses patience, and restores best weights.
Mechanisms differ: L2 shrinks all weights, dropout breaks co-adaptation, early stopping limits training time.
They can be combined for better regularization.

bank.q: Explain common dataset augmentation techniques for image classification. Compare grid search, random search, and validation-based hyperparameter tuning.
outline: Image augmentation: random flips, rotations, crops, translation, brightness/contrast changes.
All transforms must preserve the label.
Augmentation reduces overfitting by increasing data diversity.
Hyperparameters include learning rate, batch size, number of layers, regularization strength.
Grid search is exhaustive but expensive; random search is often more efficient.
Tuning uses a validation set, never the test set; cross-validation gives more reliable estimates.

bank.q: Given loss L(w) = (w − 4)², start w = 0 and learning rate η = 0.1. Perform two full-batch gradient descent updates. Then for model y = wx and squared error, compute the first mini-batch gradient and one update from samples (1,2) and (2,4) at w = 1.
outline: Derivative dL/dw = 2(w − 4).
Step 1: gradient −8, update w = 0.8.
Step 2: gradient −6.4, update w = 1.44.
For each sample error (y − wx)², derivative is −2x(y − wx).
At w = 1, sample gradients are −2 and −8; mini-batch average is −5.

bank.q: A network is trained with momentum β = 0.9 and learning rate η = 0.1. Starting from w = 0 and v = 0, the first three gradient values are 0.4, 0.6, and 0.5. Compute w after three standard momentum updates. Explain what would change in Nesterov momentum.
outline: Standard update: v ← 0.9v − 0.1g; w ← w + v.
Nesterov would compute gradient at w + βv before forming v, which can give a better direction.
With a constant gradient, standard and Nesterov updates coincide.

bank.q: Perform two Adam update steps from θ0 = 0 with gradients g1 = 0.3 and g2 = −0.2. Use β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, η = 0.1, ε = 1e−8, m0 = 0, v0 = 0.
outline: Update θ1 = −0.1 because 0.3/√0.09 = 1.
Update magnitude ≈ 0.01445; θ2 ≈ −0.11445.
Show formulas for m̂ and v̂ using 1 − β^t.

bank.q: A 20-layer network uses tanh activations and all weights are initialized from N(0, 0.01). Explain with variance reasoning why training fails. Propose and justify changes to activation, initialization, and normalization.
outline: Tanh saturates for large absolute inputs, giving derivatives close to 0.
Small initial weights give shrinking forward activations and shrinking backward gradients layer by layer.
Backprop multiplies many Jacobian factors, causing vanishing gradients.
Change tanh to ReLU to get unit derivative for positive inputs.
Use He initialization with variance 2/n_in.
Add batch normalization to stabilize scale and reduce dependence on initialization.

bank.q: Compare SGD, momentum, RMSProp, and Adam for training a large convolutional network on noisy mini-batches. Recommend a default optimizer and justify your choice using noise, adaptivity, and convergence speed.
outline: SGD is unbiased but noisy and slow; requires careful learning rate schedule.
Momentum smooths gradient noise and accelerates along consistent directions.
RMSProp normalizes by recent squared gradients, helping with nonstationary losses.
Adam combines momentum and RMSProp with bias correction; robust to noisy and sparse gradients.
For large CNNs, Adam or AdamW is a common default because it is less sensitive to the initial learning rate.
But SGD with momentum can generalize better in some settings; recommend monitoring validation.

bank.q: Design a regularization and augmentation strategy for a 5,000-image classification task with a high-capacity CNN. Justify each choice and describe how to use validation curves for early stopping.
outline: Use label-preserving augmentation: flips, crops, rotations, brightness changes to increase data diversity.
Use L2 regularization with a small λ to penalize large weights without underfitting.
Use dropout on fully connected layers to break co-adaptation.
Monitor validation loss; stop when it stops improving after a patience period and restore best weights.
Optional batch normalization adds slight regularization and speeds training.
Justify through bias-variance tradeoff: high-capacity model has low bias but high variance, so regularization reduces variance.

glossary.meaning: A scalar measure J(θ) of how far model predictions are from targets; training minimizes it.
Vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter.
Step size η used when updating parameters from gradients.
One complete pass through the full training dataset.
Number of training examples used to compute one gradient estimate.
Parameter update θ ← θ − η∇J(θ) using the full training loss.
Gradient descent update using one randomly chosen sample at a time.
Gradient descent update using a small random subset of m samples.
A moving average of past gradients added to current update to smooth and accelerate.
Momentum variant that computes the gradient at a lookahead point θ + βv.
Adaptive optimizer that divides each parameter's learning rate by the square root of its accumulated squared gradients.
Adaptive optimizer that divides by a moving average of squared gradients to prevent AdaGrad's lr decay.
Adaptive optimizer combining first and second moment estimates with bias correction.
Gradient signal disappearing as it flows backward through deep layers.
Gradient signal growing uncontrollably, causing unstable updates or NaN values.
Weight initialization with variance 2/(n_in + n_out) for tanh or sigmoid networks.
Weight initialization with variance 2/n_in for ReLU networks.
Layer that normalizes each mini-batch activation to zero mean and unit variance, then applies learnable scale and shift.
Regularization that randomly drops units during training, forcing the network not to rely on any one unit.
Adding λ Σ w² to the loss to penalize large weights.
Training until validation loss stops improving, then using the best saved model.
Generating transformed copies of training examples without changing labels.
Searching training settings such as learning rate and batch size for best validation performance.
Balance between underfitting error from bias and overfitting error from variance.
Model fits training data too closely and generalizes poorly to new data.
Ability of a trained model to perform well on unseen data.
